title: Blood Transfusion Reactions: Stop the Blood First
bottomLine: A new fever, chills, dyspnea, wheeze, chest/back/flank pain, hypotension, hives, hemoglobinuria, or acute respiratory change during transfusion is a reaction until assessed. Stop the transfusion immediately, maintain IV access with compatible normal saline using new tubing per policy, assess the patient, notify the responsible clinician and transfusion service, and follow the reaction workup.
recognize: Acute hemolytic reaction can cause fever/chills, pain, hypotension, hemoglobinuria, DIC, and AKI
Allergic reactions range from urticaria to anaphylaxis
TACO causes circulatory-overload findings such as dyspnea, hypertension, JVD, and pulmonary edema
TRALI causes acute hypoxemic noncardiogenic pulmonary edema
assess: Stop blood, then assess airway, breathing, SpO2, BP, pulse, temperature, lung sounds, urine output, and symptoms
Recheck patient and product identification with authorized staff
Document timing, product, volume infused, findings, notifications, and response
actions: Stop the transfusion; do not simply slow it
Maintain IV access with compatible normal saline/new tubing according to policy
Notify the responsible clinician and blood bank/transfusion service
Send required product/tubing/specimens and provide reaction-specific treatment as ordered
diagnostics: Reaction testing may include hemolysis studies, direct antiglobulin testing, cultures, chest imaging, or volume-status studies depending on the suspected reaction
Do not delay emergency treatment while obtaining specimens
medicationSafety: Premedication does not prevent all serious reactions and never replaces bedside monitoring
Reaction treatment is type-specific: epinephrine for anaphylaxis, diuresis for selected TACO, and supportive care for TRALI under the treatment plan
teaching: Tell the patient to report chills, itching, breathing difficulty, chest/back pain, or feeling suddenly unwell immediately during transfusion
scopeAndDelegation: LPN/LVN blood-product administration authority varies by state and facility. Regardless of who initiated the transfusion, suspected reaction requires immediate exposure cessation and escalation according to policy.
examTrap: Slowing the transfusion to see whether symptoms improve instead of stopping it.
oneLinePearl: Transfusion reaction: stop blood, keep access, assess, notify.
sourceBasis: AABB Circular of Information for the Use of Human Blood and Blood Components

title: Anemia: Oxygen Delivery, Not Just Hemoglobin
bottomLine: Anemia reduces oxygen-carrying capacity, but urgency depends on symptoms, rate of blood loss, cardiopulmonary reserve, and cause. Assess dyspnea, tachycardia, chest pain, syncope, bleeding, and functional change—not the hemoglobin number alone—and treat the cause rather than reflexively giving iron or transfusion.
recognize: Fatigue, pallor, exertional dyspnea, tachycardia, dizziness
Acute blood loss can cause shock before hemoglobin fully equilibrates
Iron deficiency, B12/folate deficiency, CKD/inflammation, hemolysis, and bleeding require different treatment
assess: Vital signs, perfusion, symptoms with activity, and bleeding history
Review stool/menstrual loss, diet, medications, renal disease, and chronic inflammation
Trend CBC indices, reticulocytes, iron studies, B12/folate, and cause-specific tests as ordered
actions: Treat active bleeding or hemodynamic instability first
Administer iron, vitamin replacement, erythropoiesis-stimulating therapy, or transfusion only when ordered for the identified problem
Reassess symptoms and laboratory response
diagnostics: MCV helps classify anemia but does not establish the cause
Ferritin may rise with inflammation, so iron studies require context
Occult blood loss requires source evaluation
medicationSafety: Oral iron commonly causes GI upset, constipation, and dark stool
IV iron can cause infusion reactions
Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents can increase thrombotic risk and require hemoglobin and BP monitoring
teaching: Take iron as directed and follow absorption instructions
Report tarry stool with weakness, hematemesis, syncope, or other bleeding symptoms rather than assuming every dark stool is from iron
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN monitors symptoms and laboratory trends and administers ordered replacement therapy. Transfusion thresholds and cause-specific treatment are clinician decisions.
examTrap: Giving iron automatically to any patient with low hemoglobin without confirming iron deficiency or another indication.
oneLinePearl: Anemia care asks: how sick, how fast, and why?
sourceBasis: American Society of Hematology anemia practice principles

title: Sickle Cell Vaso-Occlusive Crisis: Treat Pain and Find the Dangerous Complication
bottomLine: Vaso-occlusive pain requires prompt individualized analgesia and appropriate hydration; oxygen is for hypoxemia, not a ritual for every crisis. Screen every severe episode for acute chest syndrome, stroke, sepsis, splenic sequestration, or priapism because those complications immediately change the priority.
recognize: Severe bone, joint, back, abdominal, or chest pain from vaso-occlusion
Acute chest syndrome includes new respiratory symptoms with pulmonary infiltrate and may include fever or hypoxemia
Functional asplenia increases risk of severe bacterial infection
Acute focal neurologic change is a stroke emergency
assess: Pain, SpO2, respiratory effort, temperature, hydration, and neurologic status
Review the patient's usual crisis plan and baseline hemoglobin
Trend CBC/reticulocytes and complication-specific tests as ordered
actions: Give analgesia promptly using the individualized protocol
Use oral or IV fluids according to hydration and cardiopulmonary status; avoid indiscriminate overhydration
Use incentive spirometry in hospitalized vaso-occlusive pain when ordered
Escalate acute chest, stroke, sepsis, splenic sequestration, or priapism immediately
diagnostics: Obtain chest imaging for new respiratory symptoms
Transfusion is complication- and severity-specific, not automatic for every pain episode
medicationSafety: Opioid-tolerant patients may require individualized dosing plus respiratory monitoring
Hydroxyurea reduces complications for eligible patients but requires blood-count and pregnancy-safety monitoring
Avoid stigmatizing undertreatment of pain
teaching: Hydration, vaccination/infection precautions, hydroxyurea adherence when prescribed, and early emergency care for chest, neuro, fever, or priapism symptoms
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN care centers on rapid symptom recognition, protocol-directed analgesia/support, reassessment, and complication escalation. Exchange-transfusion decisions are specialty-team directed.
examTrap: Applying oxygen automatically to a normoxic patient while delaying analgesia or failing to assess new chest symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Treat the pain fast, then look for chest, brain, infection, spleen, or priapism danger.
sourceBasis: American Society of Hematology Sickle Cell Disease Guidelines

title: Thrombocytopenia and ITP: Prevent Bleeding Without Creating New Harm
bottomLine: Low platelets increase bleeding risk, but urgency depends on active bleeding, cause, trend, and clinical context. Use appropriate bleeding precautions, avoid unnecessary invasive procedures, IM injections, and rectal manipulation, and urgently escalate new neurologic symptoms, major bleeding, or hemodynamic instability.
recognize: Petechiae, purpura, ecchymosis, epistaxis, gum bleeding, heavy menses
GI, GU, or intracranial bleeding can occur
ITP is an immune thrombocytopenia diagnosis made after other causes are considered
assess: Skin/mucosa, urine/stool/emesis, headache or neuro symptoms, menstrual bleeding
Trend platelet count and the rest of the CBC
Review heparin, antiplatelets, anticoagulants, infection, liver disease, and chemotherapy
actions: Use bleeding precautions appropriate to severity
Apply prolonged gentle pressure after venipuncture
Administer corticosteroid, IVIG, or platelets only when ordered for the cause and bleeding scenario
Escalate head injury or new neurologic change
diagnostics: CBC and peripheral smear help distinguish isolated thrombocytopenia from broader marrow or systemic disease
A platelet count alone does not establish the diagnosis
medicationSafety: Avoid nonprescribed aspirin/NSAIDs when bleeding risk is high
Platelet transfusion is not routine prophylaxis for every patient with ITP
redFlags: New severe headache or neurologic deficit
Rapid platelet fall after heparin with thrombosis
teaching: Use low-trauma oral and grooming care, report head injury or bleeding, and review OTC drugs/supplements before use
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN implements bleeding precautions, trends counts, administers ordered therapy, and reports active bleeding. Treatment thresholds are hematology/provider directed.
examTrap: Putting every stable thrombocytopenic patient on strict bedrest, increasing deconditioning and VTE risk without a specific indication.
oneLinePearl: Low platelets: protect from trauma, but assess the patient and bleeding—not just the count.
sourceBasis: American Society of Hematology Immune Thrombocytopenia Guidelines

title: DIC: Clotting Everywhere, Bleeding Everywhere
bottomLine: Disseminated intravascular coagulation causes uncontrolled coagulation activation with consumption of platelets and clotting factors, producing both microvascular organ injury and bleeding. Treat the underlying cause urgently while supporting perfusion and replacing blood components when ordered for clinically significant bleeding or procedure needs.
recognize: Oozing from IV sites or wounds, petechiae, ecchymoses, GI/GU bleeding
Kidney, lung, brain, or skin injury can reflect microthrombi
Typical laboratory pattern can include falling platelets/fibrinogen, prolonged coagulation tests, and elevated D-dimer
assess: Bleeding sites, perfusion, mental status, urine output, and respiratory status
Trend CBC, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer, and organ markers
Identify sepsis, obstetric catastrophe, trauma, malignancy, or other trigger
actions: Treat the trigger as the highest priority
Minimize unnecessary invasive procedures
Administer platelets, plasma, cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen replacement, or anticoagulation only as ordered for the clinical context
Monitor for shock and organ failure
diagnostics: DIC is a clinicopathologic syndrome; no single laboratory result establishes it without the clinical context
medicationSafety: Heparin is not automatically appropriate for every bleeding DIC patient
Blood components require transfusion-reaction and volume-status monitoring
redFlags: Rapid laboratory deterioration with clinical bleeding
teaching: After stabilization, explain bleeding precautions and the underlying illness driving the coagulation problem
scopeAndDelegation: DIC is high-acuity care. PN/LVN participation depends on setting, but rapid recognition of bleeding/perfusion change and escalation are universal responsibilities.
examTrap: Replacing clotting factors while failing to address the sepsis, trauma, or obstetric event driving the DIC.
oneLinePearl: DIC treatment starts with the cause; support bleeding and organs in parallel.
sourceBasis: International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis DIC principles

title: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia: Low Platelets, High Clot Risk
bottomLine: HIT is an immune reaction to heparin characterized by a clinically important platelet fall and high thrombosis risk. When HIT is suspected, stop all heparin exposure, including flushes, and notify the team immediately; alternative non-heparin anticoagulation is often required after risk assessment.
recognize: Platelet fall often greater than 50% from baseline after heparin exposure
New thrombosis, skin necrosis, or systemic reaction after heparin
The absolute platelet count may still be above the laboratory low threshold despite a clinically important decline
assess: Review platelet trend and timing of every heparin exposure
Assess for new limb swelling/pain, chest symptoms, neurologic deficits, or line thrombosis
Identify prophylaxis, infusions, heparin-coated exposure, and flushes
actions: Stop all heparin and notify the responsible clinician
Follow validated HIT pretest probability and testing pathway
Administer an alternative anticoagulant as ordered when indicated
Evaluate for thrombosis
diagnostics: A validated score such as the 4Ts estimates pretest probability; immunoassay and functional testing are used according to the diagnostic pathway
Do not diagnose HIT from thrombocytopenia alone
medicationSafety: Do not start warfarin alone in acute HIT before platelet recovery
Platelet transfusion is generally reserved for bleeding or selected procedures rather than routine use
redFlags: Rapid platelet fall with heparin exposure
teaching: Ensure prior HIT is clearly documented and communicated to future clinicians
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN can recognize the platelet/timing pattern and hold heparin under explicit medication parameters or emergency policy while urgently notifying the prescriber. Alternative-anticoagulant selection is provider directed.
examTrap: Stopping the heparin infusion but continuing heparin flushes because they seem too small to matter.
oneLinePearl: HIT: stop every heparin source and think thrombosis.
sourceBasis: American Society of Hematology HIT Guidelines

title: Anticoagulants: Prevent Clots Without Missing the Bleed
bottomLine: Anticoagulant safety starts with indication, dose, kidney/liver function, interactions, and bleeding assessment. New severe headache, neurologic change, hemodynamic instability, GI bleeding, hematuria, or significant trauma can represent major bleeding and requires urgent evaluation—not simply holding the next dose and waiting.
recognize: Minor bruising differs from critical-site or hemodynamically important bleeding
Warfarin effect is monitored with INR; DOACs are not routinely managed by INR
Renal function materially affects several DOACs and LMWH products
assess: Skin, stool, urine, emesis, neuro symptoms, falls/trauma
Medication reconciliation for NSAIDs, antiplatelets, herbals, and interactions
CBC, renal/liver function, and drug-specific monitoring
actions: Hold and urgently notify according to order/protocol for suspected major bleeding
Use drug-specific reversal and supportive treatment as ordered
Apply bleeding precautions without unnecessary immobility
diagnostics: INR guides warfarin therapy
Normal PT/INR does not reliably exclude clinically important DOAC effect
medicationSafety: Teach consistent vitamin K intake with warfarin rather than eliminating vitamin K foods
DOAC dose depends on indication and renal function
NSAIDs and multiple antithrombotic drugs increase bleeding risk
redFlags: New severe headache or focal deficit
teaching: Take exactly as prescribed, do not double missed doses without instructions, use bleeding precautions, and tell clinicians/dentists about therapy
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN administers anticoagulants and monitors bleeding within authorized scope. Dose changes and reversal follow explicit orders or protocols.
examTrap: Teaching a warfarin patient to eliminate all leafy green vegetables instead of keeping vitamin K intake reasonably consistent.
oneLinePearl: Anticoagulant care: indication, kidney, interactions, bleeding.

title: Neutropenic Fever: Infection Can Be Quiet and Time-Critical
bottomLine: Fever in severe neutropenia is an oncologic emergency because infection can progress with few local inflammatory signs. Use the facility neutropenic-fever threshold and pathway, obtain ordered cultures promptly, and give empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics without avoidable delay.
recognize: Fever may be the only infection sign
Mucositis, central lines, GI translocation, and skin breakdown create portals of entry
Neutropenic patients may not produce pus or dramatic inflammation
assess: Vital signs, perfusion, mental status, mouth/skin/line, respiratory, urinary, and GI symptoms
Avoid traumatic rectal temperatures/exams in severe neutropenia
Trend CBC with ANC, renal/liver function, and cultures as ordered
actions: Activate neutropenic-fever/sepsis pathway
Obtain cultures before antibiotics when feasible without delaying time-critical treatment
Administer prescribed broad-spectrum therapy promptly
Use meticulous hand hygiene and indicated infection precautions
diagnostics: ANC defines neutropenia severity; imaging and site-specific cultures are symptom/pathway driven
medicationSafety: Antibiotic selection requires allergy and renal review
Growth-factor use is risk- and indication-specific
Vaccination decisions during immunosuppression follow oncology guidance
teaching: Know the oncology team's exact fever threshold and call immediately rather than masking the fever and waiting
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN recognizes fever and activates the oncology/sepsis pathway, collects ordered specimens, gives antibiotics within scope, and reassesses. Do not delay escalation while searching for a source.
examTrap: Giving acetaminophen for fever and waiting an hour to see whether the temperature falls before notifying the oncology team.
oneLinePearl: In neutropenia, fever alone is enough to act.

title: Tumor Lysis Syndrome: Potassium and Uric Acid Can Rise Fast
bottomLine: Rapid tumor-cell breakdown can cause hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hyperuricemia, and AKI. High-risk patients need preventive hydration and uric-acid-lowering therapy as ordered plus frequent labs; dysrhythmia, seizure, tetany, oliguria, or severe electrolyte change requires immediate escalation.
recognize: High-burden rapidly responsive hematologic malignancies are classic risks, although other tumors can qualify
TLS can occur spontaneously or after treatment
Symptoms include weakness, nausea, cramps, tetany, arrhythmia, seizure, and low urine output
assess: Rhythm monitoring when severe/high risk
Strict intake/output, weight, and hydration status
Trend potassium, phosphate, calcium, uric acid, creatinine, and LDH as ordered
actions: Administer ordered hydration while watching for overload
Give allopurinol or rasburicase according to risk and treatment plan
Treat severe electrolyte complications promptly
Prepare for dialysis when refractory severe metabolic/kidney complications occur
diagnostics: TLS is recognized by characteristic laboratory changes plus organ complications; frequent trending is part of prevention in high-risk patients
medicationSafety: Rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency because of hemolysis/methemoglobinemia risk
Avoid routine calcium replacement for asymptomatic hypocalcemia with marked hyperphosphatemia unless the treatment plan indicates it
teaching: Explain why frequent labs and hydration are required around therapy and report cramps, palpitations, low urine output, or neurologic symptoms
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN accurately trends labs and urine, administers preventive/emergency medications within authorized setting, and escalates metabolic changes. Rasburicase and dialysis strategy are specialty directed.
examTrap: Waiting for symptoms before reporting rapidly rising potassium in a high-risk patient after chemotherapy.
oneLinePearl: TLS: cells burst, potassium/phosphate/uric acid rise, calcium falls, heart and kidneys are threatened.

title: Chemotherapy Extravasation: Stop the Vesicant, Do Not Flush
bottomLine: Pain, burning, swelling, redness, resistance, leakage, or other site change during vesicant infusion can signal extravasation. Stop the infusion immediately, do not flush the suspected vesicant into tissue, preserve access temporarily when the drug-specific extravasation protocol calls for aspiration or antidote delivery, and obtain qualified oncology/pharmacy support.
recognize: Burning, stinging, swelling, erythema, tightness, or leakage
Loss of blood return can be concerning but does not prove extravasation by itself
Some vesicant injuries progress after the infusion stops
assess: Stop infusion, inspect and measure the site, and assess pain/neurovascular status
Identify exact drug, concentration, amount infused, and access type
Do not test patency by flushing the suspected vesicant into tissue
actions: Stop drug and disconnect tubing according to protocol
Leave the device temporarily when the protocol calls for aspiration or antidote
Notify oncology/pharmacy and use the drug-specific antidote and warm/cold-compress pathway
Document and arrange follow-up
diagnostics: Extravasation is primarily a clinical diagnosis; site measurements and photographs can support follow-up
medicationSafety: Warm versus cold compress and antidote choice are agent-specific
Never use one generic extravasation treatment for all antineoplastic agents
redFlags: Central-line extravasation with chest or neck symptoms
teaching: Tell patients to report burning, pain, pressure, swelling, or wetness immediately during infusion
scopeAndDelegation: Chemotherapy administration is specialty-competency restricted and may not be within PN/LVN scope. Any trained staff member recognizing suspected extravasation should stop the infusion and activate the protocol while qualified oncology staff take over.
examTrap: Flushing the IV to check patency after the patient reports burning during a vesicant infusion.
oneLinePearl: Extravasation: stop, do not flush, use the drug-specific protocol.
sourceBasis: 2025 ONS/ASCO Guideline on Management of Antineoplastic Extravasation

title: Malignant Spinal Cord Compression: Back Pain With Weakness or Bladder Change
bottomLine: In a patient with cancer, new severe back pain—especially with weakness, sensory change, gait difficulty, saddle symptoms, or bladder/bowel dysfunction—is metastatic spinal cord compression until urgently evaluated. Preserve neurologic function with rapid imaging and the ordered corticosteroid, radiation, or surgical pathway.
recognize: New focal or nocturnal back pain may precede neurologic deficit
Progressive weakness, sensory level, or gait change
Urinary retention and bowel dysfunction are late-danger findings
assess: Motor strength, sensation, gait when safe, and bladder/bowel symptoms
Pain location, onset, known cancer, anticoagulation, and trauma history
Fall risk and ability to transfer safely
actions: Urgent oncology/spine/neurosurgical escalation
Protect mobility/spine according to the clinical plan
Administer corticosteroid as ordered and prepare for urgent MRI and definitive therapy
diagnostics: MRI is the key imaging test for suspected malignant spinal cord compression
medicationSafety: High-dose corticosteroid can worsen glucose and infection risk
Analgesia should not delay repeated neurologic assessment
teaching: Patients with cancer should report new persistent back pain, weakness, numbness, or bladder/bowel change immediately
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN recognizes and reports the neurologic red-flag pattern, supports safe mobility, and administers ordered medication. Imaging, radiation, and surgery decisions are specialty directed.
examTrap: Treating new cancer-related back pain with PRN opioid alone while progressive leg weakness goes unreported.
oneLinePearl: Cancer plus new back pain plus neuro or bladder change is a cord emergency.

title: Superior Vena Cava Syndrome: Face and Neck Swelling Can Become an Airway Problem
bottomLine: SVC syndrome impairs venous return from the head and upper body, often from thoracic malignancy or thrombosis. Facial/neck/upper-extremity swelling, venous distention, dyspnea, cough, or headache require prompt evaluation; stridor, severe respiratory distress, syncope, or neurologic compromise makes airway/circulatory stabilization the priority.
recognize: Facial or periorbital swelling that may worsen when bending or lying flat
Neck/chest venous distention and upper-extremity swelling
Dyspnea, cough, hoarseness, headache
Severe disease can cause airway or cerebral edema
assess: Airway, respiratory effort, voice/stridor, SpO2, and neurologic status
Degree of facial and arm swelling/venous congestion
Central-line history and malignancy treatment
actions: Elevate head and provide oxygen if indicated
Urgent oncology/interventional escalation
Prepare for stenting, tumor-directed therapy, or anticoagulation according to the cause
Avoid unnecessary upper-extremity venous congestion when alternatives are available
diagnostics: Contrast CT or venous imaging defines the obstruction and cause
Tissue diagnosis matters when stable but should not delay airway stabilization
medicationSafety: Steroids and diuretics are not universally definitive; use is cause-specific
Anticoagulation is used for thrombotic causes according to the treatment plan
teaching: Report increasing swelling, breathing or voice change, severe headache, or neurologic symptoms immediately
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN monitors airway, edema, and neurologic change and supports ordered treatment. Stenting, radiation, systemic therapy, or anticoagulation strategy is specialist directed.
examTrap: Laying a severely dyspneic patient flat despite worsening upper-body venous and airway congestion.
oneLinePearl: SVC: upper-body swelling plus breathing or brain symptoms can deteriorate quickly.
